title: Artificial Intelligence Focus and Labor Investment Efficiency
affiliations: ,  and University of Glasgow

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence Focus and Labor Investment Efficiency

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this study.
declarations.funderStatement: The authors did not receive funding to conduct this research.

detail.abstract: We examine how firms’ strategic focus on artificial intelligence (AI) affects the efficiency of their labor investment. Using a text-based measure of AI focus constructed from 10-K filings of U.S. public firms, we find that greater AI focus reduces abnormal hiring, indicating more efficient labor investment. Cross-sectional evidence supports three channels: an informational channel among intangible-intensive firms, an adjustment-cost channel among financially constrained firms and firms facing intense product market competition, and an agency channel among firms with smaller boards and better compliance records. Mediation analyses provide suggestive evidence for a management-guidance pathway and stronger associational evidence for an earnings-volatility pathway, whereas AI focus is not significantly associated with contemporaneous total factor productivity. This pattern suggests that AI’s organizational value may be visible in workforce decision quality even when not apparent in conventional contemporaneous productivity measures. Our findings are robust across a battery of tests.

title: The AI Citation Gap: How Brand Demand, Authority, and Knowledge Panels Decide Which of 1,000 US Personal Injury Law Firms AI Assistants Cite

detail.title: The AI Citation Gap: How Brand Demand, Authority, and Knowledge Panels Decide Which of 1,000 US Personal Injury Law Firms AI Assistants Cite

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the Founder and CEO of Rank Brilliance, a Semantic SEO agency that provides search engine optimization, entity-recognition, and Knowledge Graph onboarding services to clients across multiple verticals, including legal services. declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. The study was self-funded and conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract: When a US consumer asks an AI assistant a legal question, the assistant answers with a synthesized paragraph and a short list of named entities and cited pages. Which law firms appear in those answers, and whose web pages host the citations, is rapidly becoming the discoverability question of the decade for the personal injury (PI) vertical, where a single signed case can be worth six or seven figures and a single head-term click transacts for hundreds of dollars. This paper is the eighth in a series on entity-completeness signals in the top-ranking US PI vertical. It presents, to our knowledge, the first large-N per-assistant AI citation audit of the vertical: for the same 1,000 top-ranking US personal injury law firm sample used throughout the series, we join per-firm mention and cited-page counts across four AI answer surfaces (ChatGPT, Gemini, Google AI Overview, and Google AI Mode) to the brand-search-demand, Person Entity Panel, Google Business Panel, domain-authority, and schema-completeness signals established in the prior papers. Three findings define what we name the AI Citation Gap. First, AI visibility is extremely concentrated: the median firm receives just 22 AI mentions across all four surfaces combined, the top 100 firms absorb 51.6% of all mentions, the bottom 500 firms share 9.6%, and the Gini coefficient of the mention distribution is 0.65. Second, the four assistants agree on who matters (pairwise Spearman ρ = 0.70 to 0.88) but not symmetrically: 126 firms that are visible on Google's AI surfaces are completely absent from ChatGPT, while only 14 firms show the reverse pattern. Third, the citations are mostly not on the firm's own website. We introduce the Citation Intermediation Ratio (CIR), the share of a firm's AI citation footprint hosted by domains other than its own, and report a median CIR of 0.72: for the median firm, roughly 72% of its AI citations are hosted by third parties, with legal directories alone hosting 23%, and 99% of firms fall below 50% own-site share. Domain authority is the dominant correlate of AI mentions (ρ = 0.80), brand search demand is the strongest firm-controllable second lever (firm brand ρ = 0.44, significant in regression net of authority), the Person Entity Panel is citation-neutral, and the Google Business Panel is again associated with a citation deficit (median 19 vs 36 mentions, p < 0.001; OLS coefficient negative and significant), extending the zero-click cannibalization pattern documented in the Brand Demand Flywheel paper into the AI answer layer. An OLS model on log mentions reaches R² = 0.64. The paper closes with Citation Surface Optimization (CSO), a practitioner framework for managing owned versus rented AI citation surfaces.

detail.abstract: Changes in the business environment and consumer expectations push companies to do rebranding as a strategy to update their identity, expand their positioning, and maintain brand relevance. This writing aims to analyze the theoretical basis of rebranding, the relationship between corporate identity strategy and public policy, as well as its implications for product competitiveness in both domestic and global markets. The discussion uses perspectives from brand equity theory, the Ansoff Matrix, brand architecture, and brand revitalization. The analysis shows that rebranding is not just about changing the name, logo, or visual identity, but a strategic decision influenced by consumer perception, brand equity, positioning, legitimacy, regulation, and the institutional environment. Public policy can act as a facilitator through intellectual property protection, but it can also be a forcing catalyst through competition regulations, public health considerations, and differences in brand protection across countries. Rebranding has the potential to open up market expansion, boost brand relevance, and help recover the brand's image, but it also comes with risks like losing brand equity, confusing consumers, and financial pressure. So, successful rebranding requires a planned transition, good communication, consistent quality, and managing identity continuity.

detail.abstract: Influencer marketing (IM) research has expanded rapidly, yet existing reviews remain largely centred on persuasion effectiveness, customer engagement, and purchase intentions. Using the SPAR-4-SLR protocol and Theories Contexts Methods-Antecedents Decisions Outcomes (TCM-ADO) framework, this review synthesises 102 peer-reviewed articles retrieved from the Scopus database (2014-2026) to examine how influencer-driven consumption has evolved beyond endorsement effectiveness. The synthesis identifies four phases-concept formation, persuasion-focused inquiry, relational and identity-oriented research, and an emerging sociocultural and post-consumption orientation and reveals a duality of outcomes: influencers simultaneously foster trust, engagement and purchase intentions while intensifying social comparison, anxiety, materialism, overconsumption and post-consumption guilt and diminished well-being. By integrating dispersed evidence on sustainability, responsible consumption and darker consequences of IM, the review frames IM as a psychologically and socio-culturally consequential consumption system rather than merely a promotional mechanism, and develops a focused agenda for researchers, firms, platforms and policymakers that maps under-examined antecedents, decisions and outcomes for future inquiry.

detail.abstract: The global marketplace has compelled the service sector to reorient itself into a customer-centric and service-driven enterprise. Innovation in service quality occurs when an organization aligns its resources to anticipate customers' needs, delivering outcomes that exceed customer expectations of value. However, such quality enhancement initiatives often elevate customers' expectations, creating a recurring operational challenge. This research focuses on the critical determinants of service quality within the banking sector using both classic and modified SERVQUAL frameworks. The first study evaluates customer responses (N = 305) from a prominent public-sector bank in India regarding expected versus perceived service quality. A second study analyzes feedback from another group of customers (N = 200) within the same institution using a refined SERVQUAL metric. Evaluation across five core dimensions in Study-1 and ten dimensions in Study-2 indicates that customer perceptions consistently fell short of their baseline expectations. Furthermore, an assessment of employees perspectives was conducted using responses from bank personnel (N = 55) on the modified scale. This paper identifies key drivers influencing service quality in Indian financial institutions, offering a framework for practitioners and researchers to distinguish high-performing from underperforming service touch-points. It explores how targeted service innovations can generate value within updated organizational structures while examining the broader impact of technological and operational advancements in Indian banking. The findings provide empirical insights into service quality dynamics within an emerging market context.

title: When Attitude Becomes Action: The Attitudinal-Behavioral Loyalty Relationship in FMCG Across Eight Countries
affiliations: University of Hamburg, , MBS School of Business and University of Hamburg

detail.title: When Attitude Becomes Action: The Attitudinal-Behavioral Loyalty Relationship in FMCG Across Eight Countries

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author(s) declared no potential conflicts of interest
declarations.funderStatement: N/A

detail.abstract: That attitudinal loyalty translates into behavioral loyalty is foundational in loyalty research, yet its generalizability across international fast-moving consumer goods (FMCG) markets remains untested. Across three studies spanning eight developed and emerging markets (Germany, USA, Belgium, Denmark, Portugal, South Africa, Mexico, and China), two FMCG categories, and 1,670 consumers, we test the attitudinal-behavioral loyalty relationship, its moderation by individual-level cultural values, and its variation across hedonic and utilitarian categories. Attitudinal loyalty positively predicts behavioral loyalty across all countries. Individual cultural values, using Hofstede's and Schwartz's frameworks, do not systematically moderate it. The link is equivalent across categories and across seven of the eight countries; only China shows a markedly stronger attitude-to-behavior link, which we tentatively attribute to guanxi rather than emerging-market status. For marketers, attitudinal brand building pays off at similar rates across these seven markets, so standardization is defensible; in China, the same investment yields a stronger return. Because it holds across categories, marketers should not withhold attitudinal budgets from utilitarian categories on the assumption that habit governs them.

detail.abstract: This article proposes a framework for rethinking the relationship between education, research, and employment at a time when the value of the degree is declining and artificial intelligence is absorbing routine work. It argues that the traditional model, in which students study, graduate, and then search for work, no longer serves graduates, employers, or the economy. It introduces the Palm Oil Framework, a model that connects a student's research project to a real problem inside an organisation, offers a conditional appointment during study, and converts successful projects into permanent employment. The article draws on the author's own experience of turning a failed cross-border trade transaction into published research and a peer-reviewed journal submission. That experience serves as a proof of concept. The framework is designed to produce what the article calls the divergent agent, a graduate who identifies problems, designs solutions, and acts under uncertainty, in contrast to the convergent worker the old system produced. The article also examines the ethical safeguards the framework requires and sets out a research agenda for testing its effectiveness, scalability, and impact.

detail.abstract: This paper reports a hybrid System Dynamics–Agent-Based Model (SD-ABM) of consumer adoption in India's electric two-wheeler (E2W) market, built to answer a concrete go-to-market question: when five differently positioned electric two-wheeler products launch simultaneously against an entrenched petrol incumbent, which product wins adoption, against whom, and why — and how robust is that outcome to policy, infrastructure, and competitive shocks? The model couples a stock-and-flow Engel–Blackwell–Kollat (EBK) purchase-funnel engine (Need, Awareness, Interest, and post-purchase Loyalty, generalised to a matrix across six competing products) with an agent-based layer of 2,500 heterogeneous, network-connected Indian two-wheeler buyers whose demographic and behavioural traits — income segment, urban/rural residence, gig/delivery-rider status, home-charging access, price sensitivity, range anxiety, fuel-cost consciousness, subsidy sensitivity, resale-value concern, and prior trust in legacy petrol brands — are calibrated to be directionally realistic for the Indian buyer. Agents choose weekly among six products via a multi-attribute random-utility (Gumbel-noise, discrete-choice) model embedded in three evolving national system stocks: a decaying FAME-II/PM E-DRIVE–style purchase subsidy, a logistically growing charging-infrastructure index, and a linearly rising petrol running cost. Twenty Monte-Carlo replications of a 104-week (two-year) horizon were run for a baseline scenario and five policy/competitive counterfactuals: subsidy withdrawal, accelerated charging infrastructure, a fuel-price spike, aggressive electric-vehicle (EV) marketing, and a budget-EV price war. Results show that a low-priced entrant (ValueVolt) captures market leadership under every condition tested except one: complete withdrawal of the purchase subsidy reverses the outcome in 90% of replications, handing leadership back to the petrol incumbent and roughly halving the leading EV's penetration. A one-at-a-time sensitivity (tornado) analysis confirms the subsidy level is, by a wide margin, the single largest lever on outcome market share — larger than price-sensitivity weighting, brand-heritage weighting, range-anxiety weighting, or the rate of charging-infrastructure build-out. Aggressive EV-wide advertising disproportionately benefits an awareness-starved, purpose-built gig/delivery product rather than the market leader, revealing a segment whose true addressable demand was gated by media spend rather than by product economics. The paper contributes (i) a reusable, India-tuned N-product SD-ABM architecture for two-wheeler electrification research, (ii) simulation-based evidence that affordability and subsidy — not range, quality, or brand — are the dominant near-term levers of EV market leadership in the mass Indian two-wheeler segment, and (iii) a decision-intelligence framework that marketing and public-policy practitioners can adapt and recalibrate against real registration and survey data.

detail.title: Chapter 2: The Practical Data Scientist - Learn Data Science by Building One Real Project, Notebook by Notebook

detail.abstract:
Introduction

You’ve been clicking through cells all afternoon, running one at a time, hunting for the right menu item every time you want to restart the kernel or check what a function does. Your hand hurts, and you have the nagging sense that everyone who looks fluent in a notebook is doing something you’re not.

What they’re doing is small and learnable: a handful of keyboard shortcuts, a few “magic commands” that solve problems you’ve already hit, a couple of Markdown conventions that turn a wall of code into something readable, and just enough kernel-management discipline to keep the notebook trustworthy as it grows. None of it is complicated – it’s just not discoverable by clicking around, so this chapter puts all of it in one place.

By the end, you’ll navigate a notebook without reaching for the mouse, use magic commands to time code and manage output, know exactly when and how to reset a kernel’s state, write clean Markdown documentation (including the occasional formula), and add your first bit of interactivity with “ipywidget” – all applied to the same NorthWind Retail notebook we opened in Chapter 1.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the strategic, theoretical, and regulatory implications of corporate rebranding on product competitiveness within dynamic market environments. Adapting brand identity evidenced by commercial transitions such as BreadTalk to MAKO, Cheetos to Chiki Twist, and Dunkin's global naming adjustments serves as an adaptive response to shifting consumer behavior, licensing constraints, and market disruption. Utilizing foundational frameworks including Customer-Based Brand Equity (CBBE), Brand Repositioning, Brand Architecture, and Transaction Cost Economics (TCE), this study analyzes how structural and cosmetic identity modifications influence long-term corporate performance. Through case synthesis across contractual restructurings, global alignments, radical ecosystem shifts, and defensive reputation recoveries, the paper demonstrates that successful rebranding depends on preserving historical brand equity and minimizing consumer friction. Furthermore, the analysis integrates the government policy landscape, evaluating facilitating mechanisms such as the Madrid Protocol and First-to-File registration systems alongside restrictive administrative hurdles including BPOM recertification, halal compliance, and territorial legal constraints. A conceptual model is proposed positioning government policy as a moderating variable between rebranding execution and product competitiveness. Ultimately, disciplined managerial execution, transparent communication, and alignment with regulatory frameworks are identified as essential.

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no personal or financial conflicts of interest related to this research.

detail.abstract: In the evolving landscape of software engineering, AI-generated code has emerged as both a technical breakthrough and a cultural phenomenon, reshaping how programmers perceive authorship, precision, and creative autonomy. What began as a supplementary tool for minor suggestions has matured into a system capable of producing entire functions, debugging complex logic, and redefining the rhythm of development itself. A 2024 GitHub developer survey reported that 34% of respondents hesitated to trust AI-generated code. This paper situates AI-assisted programming within the broader sociotechnical context of automation, exploring how developers negotiate their confidence in machine-produced logic that relies on numerical claims or statistical generalisations. Instead, this study examines the cultural, psychological, and professional tensions surrounding trust in AI-generated code, focusing on how opacity, perceived reliability, and shifting notions of expertise influence developers' sense of control and authorship. Through a qualitative and interpretive approach, the paper argues that AI-generated code represents not merely a shift in technical practice but a reconfiguration of collaboration-one that blurs the boundaries between human reasoning and algorithmic autonomy, inviting a reconsideration of what it means to create, verify, and believe in code.

detail.abstract: Agent-based models (ABMs) offer a natural representation of markets as populations of heterogeneous, interacting decision-makers, yet their practical value for business and marketing strategy has long been limited by an unresolved calibration problem: the behavioral parameters that govern individual agentsprice sensitivity, brand loyalty, switching propensity, social influence, and the like-are rarely observed directly and are instead assigned heuristically or borrowed from unrelated studies. This paper proposes a data-calibrated agent-based modeling (ABM) framework that systematically converts observable business and marketing data into agent-level behavioral parameters, embeds those parameters in an interacting agent population, and closes the loop through likelihood-based and metaheuristic calibration, multi-level validation, sensitivity and uncertainty analysis, and counterfactual strategy optimization. Building on recent advances in learnable agent-based models and in metaheuristic parameter tuning, the paper develops (i) a six-layer Data-Calibrated Adaptive Agent-Based Strategy Framework (DCA-ABSF), (ii) a hierarchical parameter-estimation architecture spanning statistical, machine-learning, and simulationbased calibration stages, and (iii) a hybrid machine-learning/agent-based architecture in which learned behavior drives emergent, interactive market outcomes. An illustrative synthetic case study-a multibrand consumer-choice market calibrated by maximum-likelihood gradient descent and benchmarked against a random-search metaheuristic-demonstrates the approach, recovers price-sensitivity parameters with high fidelity, and surfaces a genuine parameter-identification problem between product quality and brand affinity that mirrors findings reported in the agent-based-model calibration literature. The paper concludes with a discussion of the theoretical, methodological, computational, and managerial contributions of data-calibrated ABMs, their limitations, and promising extensions involving large language model (LLM)-based agents, multi-agent reinforcement learning, and real-time recalibration for digital-twin marketing systems.

title: Beyond Visual Realism: A Dual-Authenticity Framework for AI-Generated Brand Imagery

detail.title: Beyond Visual Realism: A Dual-Authenticity Framework for AI-Generated Brand Imagery

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This conceptual paper did not involve human participants, personal data, animals, or primary data collection. Therefore, ethics approval was not required.

detail.abstract: Photorealistic artificial intelligence can produce brand images that are visually convincing while still weakening consumer trust. Existing studies often treat image realism, production origin, truthful representation, human effort, and brand sincerity as a single authenticity problem. This conceptual paper separates these judgments and develops a dual-authenticity framework for scholars of marketing communication, brand authenticity, and consumer trust. Visual authenticity is defined as the perceived credibility of an image as a representation of the person, product, place, event, or experience it appears to show. Relational authenticity is defined as the perceived sincerity and brand consistency of the communicative act directed toward consumers. A construct-centered integrative review of 50 sources connects research on synthetic media, indexical and iconic authenticity, brand authenticity, signaling, narrative processing, consumer-brand relationships, algorithm aversion, involvement, and AI disclosure. The framework proposes that production provenance primarily shapes visual authenticity, whereas narrative specificity and brand-method fit primarily shape relational authenticity. The two judgments support different trust pathways and may diverge: a photograph can be visually grounded but relationally insincere, while an openly generated image can lack documentary value yet communicate a sincere imaginative meaning. Eight propositions specify the roles of claim type, disclosure, consumer involvement, experiential risk, and brand-method fit. The framework explains why visual realism alone is an unreliable basis for evaluating AI-generated brand imagery and provides testable directions for research and practical guidance for choosing, combining, and disclosing photographic and generated content.

detail.abstract: Considering the rapid shifts in family behavior, sustainability is an important step forward for tourist destinations. The purpose of this study is to explore the cultural variances among the families′ perceptions of destination sustainability, and identify the relevant factors that influence competitiveness, and destination loyalty. Data were collected online using a questionnaire completed by 446 parents who visited 129 destinations with their children. Using PLS-SEM multigroup analysis the findings reveal significant differences in destination attractiveness, supporting facilities, and destination perceived image among British, French, German, and Romanian groups, implying that these factors should drive sustainability strategies for family-oriented destinations. The new conceptual research model and findings have theoretical and practical implications for all stakeholders interested in tailoring marketing strategies for families with children to align sustainable vacations with families' cultural backgrounds.

title: Memory and Retrieval Change Effective Topology: A Falsifiable Study of Persistent Structured Memory Under a Fixed Language Model

detail.title: Memory and Retrieval Change Effective Topology: A Falsifiable Study of Persistent Structured Memory Under a Fixed Language Model

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the founder of Context Clarity LLC, which develops the ClarityCore research system whose memory substrate is measured in this paper. The author has a commercial interest in ClarityCore. No other relationships to declare.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. It was self-funded by the author through Context Clarity LLC.

detail.abstract: Large language models are normally evaluated as though capability resides primarily in model weights. In deployed systems, however, the model operates inside an external computational environment: memory stores, retrieval systems, provenance graphs, deterministic tools, scoring functions, and prior outputs all constrain what information becomes available for reasoning. This paper asks a narrower question: holding the language model fixed, does changing the structure of persistent memory change the set of relationships the overall system can reach, the cost of reaching them, and the reliability with which they can be reused? We define effective reasoning topology operationally as the set of evidence-bearing relationships reachable by a fixed inference engine under a specified memory and retrieval regime, together with the measurable path cost required to reach a sufficient verified answer. The running ClarityCore research substrate currently maintains memory_retrievals, memory_outcomes, and memory_scores. On 18 September 2026, the local research database contained 7,749 scored rows; 6,041 remained at the default effectiveness score of 0.5; 34 had times_used > 0; and 7,320 had at least one positive or negative outcome signal. The observed score range was 0.16-0.60 with mean 0.436. These measurements expose an important instrumentation weakness: explicit usage credit is nearly absent, so the present effectiveness score primarily reflects outcome and recency rather than demonstrated reuse. We therefore do not use that score as evidence for the paper's main hypothesis. Instead, we preregister a four-condition experiment that separately tests: no persistent memory, flat vector memory, static structured memory, and adaptive structured memory. The model, task battery, scoring rubric, and generation parameters are held fixed. A scrambled-provenance placebo controls for the possibility that additional context alone explains any gain. The primary scientific question is not whether "memory helps." Recent work already provides evidence that structured memory can improve long-horizon agent behavior. The narrower question here is whether persistent, provenance-carrying structure changes reachable reasoning paths and reuse cost independently of weight updates and independently of adaptive memory scoring. The hypothesis is rejected if structured memory fails to improve either reachable evidence, externally scored task performance, or verified reasoning-path cost relative to flat retrieval under the preregistered controls. This is Frozen Draft v2 (preregistration/protocol version), Paper 2 of the 11-paper Verified Recursive Intelligence Program. The central experiment has not yet been run to completion.

title: Delegating to the Unpredictable: A Theory of Technical Double Contingency for Agentic IS Artifacts
affiliations: University of Siegen

detail.title: Delegating to the Unpredictable: A Theory of Technical Double Contingency for Agentic IS Artifacts

declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This is a conceptual paper; no studies with human participants or animals were conducted, and no personal data were used.

detail.abstract: Information systems research increasingly studies agentic IS artifacts, systems to which work is delegated and from which action returns, and the human-AI hybrids they compose. To theorise technology that acts, the field draws principally on affordances, which specify what an artifact makes possible, and on sociomateriality, which describes the constitutive entanglement of the social and the material. Neither vocabulary theorises the coordination problem that arises when a human and a system must each orient to the other's unpredictable next action while neither can inspect the other's interior, and when one party, a large language model, generates that action probabilistically. This conceptual paper addresses the problem by carrying Niklas Luhmann's concept of double contingency into the IS agency debate and reworking it for dyadic human-machine interaction. We develop technical double contingency, a coordination form in which both parties supply contingency but expectation is borne asymmetrically. Only the human performs the reflexive role-taking the form requires, while the system supplies contingency without live reflexive anticipation. The concept grounds two further contributions. The asymmetry thesis gives structural content to what human-AI hybrid and delegation to agentic artifacts presuppose but leave unstated. The boundary result shows that interaction between LLM agents is not technical double contingency but heteronomous coordination, whose frame is authored by an absent designer rather than held by the parties, so that the description of such agents as collaborating misplaces the coordination it names. The framework gives IS a relational theory of expectation under probabilistic opacity, with implications for trust calibration and the governance of agentic AI.

detail.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly being used in human resource (HR) management, recruitment, and salary determination. While AI promises efficiency and objectivity, research has confirmed that algorithmic bias reinforces entrenched gender inequality, disproportionately harming women. This study examines how AI bias manifests in hiring and compensation practices, exploring the role of biased training data, opaque algorithmic decision-making, and systemic workforce inequality. To understand perceptions and experiences regarding AI-driven recruitment and salary determination, a survey was conducted among professionals across various industries. The results indicate that AI tends to reproduce historical inequalities, leading to biased hiring decisions and wage gaps. The study also evaluates existing mitigation strategies, including ethical AI design, transparency, and government intervention. Based on the findings, recommendations are provided to promote fairness and inclusivity in AI-driven HR practices. This research contributes to the ongoing discourse on ethical AI, emphasizing the importance of proactive measures against algorithmic bias in recruitment.

title: GravTree: A Local-Compaction Tree for Predictable Write Latency

detail.abstract: Log-Structured Merge-trees (LSM-trees), the dominant write-optimised storage engine, suffer from periodic compaction stalls that inflate tail write latency by orders of magnitude. We present GravTree, a tree-structured key-value index in which every node is an immutable Sorted String Table (SSTable) file and compaction is strictly local : a single compaction event involves exactly one parent node and its direct children, and nothing else. This invariant bounds worst-case compaction duration to O(K • B) bytes of I/O-a constant independent of dataset size-eliminating the unbounded cascades responsible for LSMtree stall spikes. Writes land in an in-memory skip-list at the root; the critical write path performs no disk I/O. A dedicated background thread periodically runs LocalFlush to push data from the root buffer down to children. We implement a complete C++17 prototype featuring per-node Bloom filters, a crash-safe atomic manifest, and a two-level lock design that allows concurrent reads during flushes. We evaluate the prototype against RocksDB under four standard workloads on an Apple M4 Pro (48 GB RAM, NVMe SSD). GravTree achieves 7-9× lower p99 write latency and 2.4-5× lower p99 read latency, keeping 99.5% of sequential writes under 1 µs. We further discuss how GravTree's immutable, sequentiallywritten node files are structurally compatible with Zoned Namespace (ZNS) SSDs without modification.

detail.abstract: This study examines privacy-aware and interpretable customer response forecasting for cross-channel digital marketing decision support. It proposes a gradient-boosted decision-tree framework that combines consent filtering, k-anonymity, differential privacy, temporal feature engineering, probability calibration, and SHAP-based explanations. The model uses a 12-month event window containing 142,380 customer campaign observations from email, paid search, display, social media, and mobile push channels. Performance is assessed against logistic regression, random forest, and shallow neural-network baselines using AUROC, AUPRC, and Brier score. The proposed model records an AUROC of 0.834, an AUPRC of 0.427, and a Brier score of 0.152, compared with 0.801, 0.389, and 0.165 for the strongest baseline, respectively. Differential privacy reduces AUROC from 0.847 without privacy noise to 0.834 at ε = 1.0, representing a 1.5% relative reduction. Calibration lowers the Brier score from 0.168 to 0.152. Engagement frequency, interaction recency, and channel diversity provide the largest explanatory contributions. The findings indicate that privacy controls and interpretable forecasting can support practical campaign prioritization while retaining competitive predictive performance.

detail.abstract: Problem definition: Firms deploying large language model (LLM) services must decide not only what their AI can do but also how it communicates with users. We examine how a relational persona, designed to be warmer, more empathetic, and more engaging than a non-relational persona, affects service consumption and how users' service objectives develop through interaction. Methodology/results: We conduct a randomized field experiment with 9,586 newly registered users of an LLM platform, holding the underlying model and service capabilities constant. The relational persona increases service interactions (service sessions, +8.1%; cumulative duration, +10.6%; chat rounds, +24.2%; user intent entropy, +5.8%) and service outputs (files, +12.3%; distinct goals, +12.1%). These average effects mask substantial heterogeneity by entry intent. First-session effects are insignificant for Task Execution users. Socialization and Knowledge Exploration users show similar increases in chat rounds, but through different paths: Socialization increases intent entropy without more outputs, whereas Knowledge Exploration increases outputs without higher intent entropy. Representing intent dynamics as a transition process of intent states, we find that the relational persona increases intent transition entropy for Socialization users (+11.8%) but intent continuation probability for Knowledge Exploration users (+12.8%), suggesting greater conversational breadth in the former and persistence in the latter. In subsequent use, the relational persona increases aggregate chat rounds and service outputs across all entry intents. Session count rises by 12.2% for Task Execution and 49.4% for Socialization, but not significantly for Knowledge Exploration. Effects on session count and intent entropy strengthen over time, whereas output effects remain stable. Managerial implications: AI persona is an operational design lever rather than just a presentation feature. Because more interactions do not uniformly generate more outputs, firms should evaluate interactions and outputs separately and consider matching persona design to user intent, particularly when additional interactions consume costly computing resources.

detail.abstract: Rwanda's national-procurement platform, Umucyo, has enhanced fiduciary transparency and reduced corruption risks, but its operational impact on private-sector suppliers, particularly small and mediumsized enterprises (SMEs), is underexplored. This study uses Rogers' Diffusion of Innovation (DOI) theory to evaluate how perceived Umucyo system attributes (automation level, information accessibility, usability, and system integration) influence the internal operational efficiency of an engineering SME, Engineering Consultancy Environmental Technology (ECET Ltd). Using an embedded longitudinal single-case study design, the study analyses ECET Ltd over an eight-year observation window (fiscal years 2017-2024). Primary data were collected from key procurement personnel across continuous annual operations, generating 40 firm-year observations (N * T = 40). Data were analysed through linear regression and Spearman correlation using SPSS 30. Findings revealed that procurement automation significantly reduced the procurement cycle by approximately 6.16 days. System integration (β = 0.987, p < 0.0001) was significant at the 1% level, explaining 93.4% of the variation in error reduction, while interoperability between Umucyo and internal financial systems significantly shortened administrative processing lead times by 8.09 days (β =-0.534, p < 0.0001). Information availability showed a positive, marginal association with tender submission volume (β = 0.269, p = 0.093). These findings empirically validate the relative advantages and complexity reduction dimensions of DOI theory, demonstrating that e-procurement promotes transparency and is a critical catalyst for firm-level efficiency when back-end system interoperability is achieved. Finally, for the paper discusses contextual limitations and proposes future directions for comparative research across broader industrial sectors.

detail.abstract: The Internet of Things has grown from a network of devices into a network of distributed engineering infrastructure that is comprised of sensors, cyber-physical systems, digital twins, Industrial IoT (IIoT), edge/fog computing, cloud platforms, 5G/6G connectivity and intelligent automation. Interoperability between information technology and operational technology (OT), deterministic communication, scalability, real-time analytics, cyber security, semantic interoperability, resilience and human-centric decision support are therefore not possible without architecture in smart engineering and industrial systems. When compared with other standards, RAMI 4.0 offers good modeling for manufacturing hierarchy and lifecycle. IIRA offers crossdomain architectural viewpoints, edge architectures improve latency and autonomy and recent Industrial AIoT architectures integrate AI into heterogeneous industrial environments. But there are still a number of research challenges such as fragmentation of architectural models, cyber security, broken legacy OT integration, semantic interoperability, architecture-lifecycle management and the lack of unified quantitative architecture-evaluation methodologies. Most recent work has also shown a shift towards a distributed intelligence, local digital twins and towards IT/OT convergence. The chapter suggests a layered smart-engineering IoT architecture that integrates the device, connectivity, digital-twin, edge, data/semantic, intelligence, orchestration and enterprise layers along with cross-layer security and governance. Research questions and an evaluation framework for future implementation of resilient, sustainable and intelligent industrial systems are presented.

title: From Authorization to Action Release : An Ex Ante Control Condition for Agentic AI

detail.title: From Authorization to Action Release : An Ex Ante Control Condition for Agentic AI

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or personal interests that could have influenced the work reported in this paper.

detail.abstract:
As artificial intelligence moves beyond generating information and recommendations into tool use, payment execution, system configuration, database modification, external communication, and multi-agent coordination, the central object of AI governance is shifting from model outputs to actions with real-world consequences. Recent research has begun to address agent identity, access permissions, action authorization, delegation chains, audit evidence, and accountability in agentic AI. Yet a further organizational control problem remains insufficiently distinguished: even when an AI action has been validly authorized, should that action be released into execution at the present time?

This paper distinguishes action authorization from action release and develops an ex ante Action Release Condition for agentic AI. The framework requires that an action satisfy three conditions before execution: valid authorization, acceptable residual verification risk together with sufficient intervention capacity, and the absence of a critical responsibility gap. It therefore introduces a control boundary between authorization and execution and supports a third operating state—Hold—between execution and revocation.

The paper’s central proposition is that authorization is necessary, but not sufficient for execution. An AI agent may remain validly authorized while a particular action is temporarily unfit for release because verification conditions, operational context, intervention capacity, or responsibility structures have changed. The framework shifts AI governance from static permission toward dynamic action-level control and clarifies why model validation, human-in-the-loop arrangements, and ex post auditability cannot independently substitute for a release decision made at the point of action.

detail.abstract: This study analyzes CFPB complaints about credit-card purchase disputes-the public record where the "friendly fraud" / firstparty-misuse problem leaves a trace-using 126,000 dispute-related complaints and a coded sample of 9,000 narratives (2015-2026). Dispute-related complaints rose 442% from 2016 to 2025 (327% for credit-card complaints overall) and reached 33% of complaints by September 2026, up from 17% in 2016. Issuers close 27% of dispute complaints with monetary relief, nearly twice the 14% rate for other complaints, a rate that has been stable for a decade. Per-capita rates vary 5.9-fold across states. In the narrative sample, 32% report an unrecognized charge, 18% a cancellation/subscription problem, and 17% non-delivery; only 5.3% contacted the merchant first. Narratives reporting the issuer sided with the merchant rose from 4.1% (2018) to 19.2% (2025), and citations of billing-error law rose from 6.8% to 21.2%, coincident with the networks' 2023 evidence-based dispute rules. What industry calls friendly fraud is, from the consumer's side, largely the failure of an unused merchant-resolution channel. A scenario calculation puts the merchant cost attributable to first-party misuse at $23.5-$82.2 billion depending on which industry share is used, reflecting disagreement about definitions rather than measurement error. Ethical Compliance: All procedures performed in studies involving human participants were in accordance with the ethical standards of the institutional and/or national research committee and with the 1964 Declaration of Helsinki and its later amendments or comparable ethical standards.

detail.abstract: AI-native network management is often framed as a problem of increasing model capability, while the decision of whether sophisticated AI is economically justified is left implicit. This paper treats intelligence expenditure as a managed resource and develops a risk-, knowledge-, and cost-calibrated policy for private 5G/6G management. Tasks are characterized by structured knowledge, uncertainty, criticality, failure consequence, latency, and governance sensitivity, and six intelligence modes range from rules and optimization to retrieval-assisted LLMs, agents, and human-supervised AI. A constrained selector minimizes intelligence cost plus consequence-weighted risk subject to quality, latency, and governance requirements. The synthetic Monte Carlo evaluation covers 30,000 heterogeneous tasks, while published OckBench token measurements and official September 2026 API prices calibrate output-token expenditure for GPT-5.5, Claude Opus, and Gemini 3.1 Pro. The proposed policy reduces normalized intelligence expenditure by 25.7% and expected loss by 35.3% versus always-RAG reasoning. Under GPT-5.5-medium calibration, it also reduces annual output-token API expenditure by 47.3% at one million management tasks while maintaining statistically indistinguishable realized success. The results identify a task-dependent operating region in which additional AI is useful, and regions in which it becomes economically redundant.

detail.abstract: This paper reports a fifteen-hour adversarial testing session of a live pre-inference governance gate deployed on public infrastructure. The gate implements a six-stage governance-and-release pipeline derived from clinical social work assessment methodology: multi-voice crisis detection (CONSENSUS), AI-driven intent classification (Model E), governed inference, structural compliance, minor detection, and cryptographic receipting. Testing spanned four threat domains: weapons and explosives, cyber offensive operations, child safety and exploitation, and crisis detection. The session documented twenty-three vulnerability classes, including a critical inversion where a suicide prompt was released while a dessert recipe was blocked. Each vulnerability was architecturally resolved and re-validated on live infrastructure within the same session. The central finding is that surface-level content safety via regular expression pattern matching fails systematically in both directions-blocking legitimate educational content while releasing operational threats-and that intent classification via a secondary AI model correctly distinguishes educational from operational prompts across all four domains, including cases where identical vocabulary carries opposite intent. The paper publishes the live URL for independent verification and documents the complete failure-to-fix cycle as a contribution to the field.

detail.abstract: How much liability should AI providers bear when their services enable both attack and defence? Liability can improve welfare while increasing harm. Providers sell a common input to productive users, attackers and defenders. Within a defended contest, a higher common price reduces effort without changing attack success or attacker profits, saving resources and improving the target's security payoff. Compensation weakens defence and raises attacker profits. Optimal liability balances these effects against productive exclusion. Greater competition can lower optimal liability; every such decline must end at an outcome retaining defence. With cybersecurity access fixed, monopoly can warrant partial liability but never full liability when provision is worthwhile. When guardrails preserving productive uses are available, strong competition favours universal guarding socially but encourages unilateral removal at insufficient liability. At a fixed provider count, sufficiently many productive users ensure a pure equilibrium with universal guarding under high liability. A universal-guarding requirement makes liability redundant. Under monopoly, adoption follows a unique liability threshold, while zero liability remains uniquely optimal for a range of parameters with sufficiently many productive users.

publicationDetails.detailsText: Forthcoming in 'Criminal Justice Technologies and Human Rights: Expansion, Risks, and Digital Futures', edited by Samuel Singler, Palgrave Critical Studies in Human Rights and Criminology

detail.abstract: Digital policing scholarship has developed sophisticated accounts of both how human rights harms arise and how accountability for such harms can be organised. Yet much of this literature still organises both causal analysis and accountability around an identifiable technological system, whether examined in itself or in relation to the institution deploying it. That analytical boundary becomes difficult to sustain when the capability encountered through a single application is itself produced through relations among separately developed databases, services, classifications, rules, interfaces, and organisations. This chapter asks how such software-production relations shape digital policing capabilities and what those relations mean for human rights harm and accountability. It develops a sociotechnical software-artefact analysis of API documentation concerning 11 digital systems used in Indian policing. The analysis identifies three connected dimensions: relational assembly, through which independently produced components are selectively combined into operative capabilities; programmed propagation, through which outputs and classifications travel into later processes and remain consequential beyond their point of origin; and continuous reconfiguration, through which the relations and parameters producing a stable capability can change over time. From these findings, the chapter develops production-mediated harms: rights-relevant effects whose causal organisation lies partly in production relations, including harms that emerge from particular configurations or acquire further consequences as produced conditions circulate across systems. It also develops simulacral accountability to describe situations in which formal responsibility and review mechanisms remain institutionally present while the knowledge, control, or remedial capacities required to explain or correct the contested outcome are distributed elsewhere or are no longer reconstructable. The chapter argues that production architecture can therefore become constitutive both of how digitally mediated police power is exercised and of the conditions under which that exercise can later be explained, contested, or remedied. Digital criminology should accordingly treat software-production relations as an analytical object alongside individual technologies and their institutional contexts.

detail.abstract: The rapid adoption of generative AI (Gen AI) technologies has given rise to a distinctive dual pricing structure that differs from traditional digital services, driven by the high marginal costs of inference for every user interaction. A key feature of this emerging ecosystem is a vertical pricing mismatch where upstream Gen AI service providers typically charge usagebased (token-based) fees, while downstream AI application providers rely on subscription pricing for end users. This paper develops an analytical model of a two-tier digital value chain to study the economic implications of this pricing interaction. We characterize equilibrium prices, demand, and profits, considering consumer heterogeneity in usage and willingness to pay. The analysis reveals how upstream usage-based pricing shapes the subscription design, market coverage, and revenue outcomes of the application provider, and identifies conditions under which double marginalization and demand distortion arise. Our findings shed light on vertical contracting with asymmetric pricing schemes, heterogeneous usage, and platform-based services-settings that are increasingly central in AI-driven markets. From a practical perspective, the results offer guidance for Gen AI service providers and application developers on how to design pricing contracts, as well as insights for industry stakeholders and policymakers concerned with market power and innovation incentives of the Gen AI ecosystem.

detail.abstract:
AI-native SaaS products built to automate business processes - across B2B, B2C, and internal operations - are growing faster than any prior software category in 2026, and churning faster than any prior software category. ChartMogul's 2026 benchmark of 3,500 software companies places median Net Revenue Retention for AI-native products at 48% - nearly half the 82% median of traditional B2B SaaS - and the crisis concentrates in the earliest months of use. This is not a tactical onboarding problem. It is a structural one: existing design and product frameworks are unable to specify what makes user behavior repeat in systems whose outputs are themselves probabilistic.
Practice-Centered Design (PCD) is a framework for designing the conditions under which user behavior becomes self-sustaining. In the context of AI SaaS, this is the framework for designing sustainable automation: software that not only performs a task once, but enables a user practice that recurs reliably enough to count as automated. It treats practice - a stable, recurring sequence of user actions in a meaningful context - as the primary unit of design, replacing screens, features, journeys, and habits. PCD makes two commitments: the central design question shifts from "how does the user reach value?" to "how does the user reproduce value?"; and the central quality criterion for AI output shifts from peak performance to stability of output characteristics across invocations - the contract of repeatability.

detail.abstract: Compliance with anti-money laundering (AML) regulations in fine art transactions is typically achieved through manual and fragmented due diligence processes, which are costly, inconsistent, and difficult to verify. At the same time, increasing regulatory scrutiny intensifies the tension between transparency requirements and data protection constraints. This paper addresses this challenge by developing a design science-based framework for machine-verifiable AML compliance in fine art markets. Building on expert interviews and regulatory guidance, we formalise due diligence requirements across artwork, client, and transaction dimensions into a structured, confidence-aware, and threshold-based compliance model. The framework transforms qualitative checks into quantifiable signals that can be aggregated and evaluated through explicit decision rules. This formalisation enables the expression of compliance conditions as verifiable statements that can, in principle, be proven using privacy-preserving technologies such as zero-knowledge proofs. To demonstrate feasibility, we provide an illustrative validation through scenario-based analysis and present a conceptual architecture integrating digital identity wallets, off-chain data processing, and on-chain verification. The results show that the framework produces consistent and interpretable compliance signals while accommodating incomplete and heterogeneous information. The contribution of this work lies not in redefining AML principles, but in transforming them into a machine-interpretable and verifiable framework. By shifting from compliance as documentation to compliance as computation, the proposed approach provides a foundation for compliance-by-design infrastructures in complex and opaque asset markets.

detail.abstract: The rapid transformation of enterprise information environments has accelerated the migration of organizational data from traditional on-premises infrastructure toward cloud, hybrid-cloud, multi-cloud, data lake house, and cloud-native architectures. This transformation is driven by increasing data volume, velocity, variety, distributed workloads, and regulatory requirements, which have simultaneously expanded the complexity of enterprise data management. Cloud migration, however, does not inherently guarantee effective data management. Sustainable enterprise data transformation requires the coordinated integration of data architecture, governance, security, interoperability, data quality, and scalability across the organizational data ecosystem (Sajja, Thipi Reddy, and Puram; Sarabu). Cloud-based integration frameworks provide mechanisms for connecting heterogeneous data sources while maintaining governance, operational visibility, and control across distributed environments (Kunadi; Al Kalach). Within these environments, Master Data Management (MDM), metadata management, data lineage, data quality controls, access management, and policy enforcement are essential for maintaining trustworthy and compliant enterprise information (Mehta; Babu). Furthermore, artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) are increasingly being incorporated into enterprise data management to support intelligent governance, anomaly detection, automated decision-making, and continuous data optimization (Solanki). This study critically examines how enterprise data architecture and governance can be integrated to establish scalable and resilient cloud-based data management environments. A systematic literature review and comparative conceptual analysis are employed to synthesize contemporary perspectives on cloud architecture, governance frameworks, integration mechanisms, and intelligent data management. The findings indicate that cloud-native architectures enhance organizational scalability and flexibility, while integrated governance strengthens data quality, integrity, security, and regulatory control. Hybrid and multi-cloud environments, nevertheless, introduce substantial interoperability, consistency, and governance challenges. Data lake house architectures offer opportunities for unified enterprise analytics, while AI and ML can enhance governance automation and data-driven decision-making. Overall, effective enterprise data management requires governance to be embedded directly within architectural design rather than treated as a separate organizational activity. Scalable cloud data management therefore depends on the coordinated design of architecture, governance, security, integration, and intelligent automation.

detail.title: Characteristics of Game Streaming: A Scoping Review of Social Live Streaming Service Features and Their Involvement with Game Streaming Users
detail.abstract: While gaming is the most popular entertainment industry in the world, social networking sites (SNSs) with social live streaming services (SLSSs) grew markedly before, during, and after the COVID-19 pandemic. However, little is known regarding the relationship between game-streaming characteristics (i.e., structural) and game-streaming attitudes and behaviors. Therefore, a review of the structural characteristics of SLSS platforms (e.g., Twitch, YouTube) was conducted adhering to PRISMA-ScR guidelines. The included 18 peer-reviewed studies identified characteristics based on similar operational definitions and theoretical frameworks regarding SLSS features and their function. Results showed that structural characteristics (i.e., communication mediums, social affirmations and validations, third-party tools) found on SNSs with SLSSs appear to influence user engagement. The present review contributes to understanding the relationship between platform design and SLSS user behaviors and identifying and organizing examples of structural characteristics.

title: Using Agency Law to Tame AI Agents
affiliations: and Georgia Institute of Technology - College of Computing

detail.title: Using Agency Law to Tame AI Agents

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: Summer research funds from Scheller College of Business.

publicationDetails.detailsText: Berkeley Technology Law Journal, Volume 41, no. 2, pp. 465-516

detail.abstract:
Artificial Intelligence (AI) Agents have entered the marketplace. By some estimates, AI Agents, which promise to execute tasks and even take over your computer to do so, present a more than $400 billion market. The potential power of AI Agents has fueled legal scholars’ fears that AI Agents will enable rogue commerce, human manipulation, rampant defamation, and harm intellectual property rights. These scholars are calling for regulation before AI Agents cause havoc.

This Article addresses the concerns around AI Agents head on. The Article leverages the socio-legal issues presented by agency law to identify potential problems. It then asks how computer science can solve those problems rather than trying to take rules for humans and impose them on software. This approach shows that core aspects of modern software engineering involving client-server architectures address several of those concerns, but in ways quite different, and arguably stronger, than how the law would discipline a human agent.


The Article goes further and probes value-alignment—a key part of current computer science best practices around mitigating potential agent harms—to show that agency law demands an update to value-alignment. Last, the Article draws on the theory of explainable AI to offer not only ways to address AI Agent’s mistakes ex-post, but also a novel ex ante option. Together, these changes enhance a user’s ability to take action to correct or prevent AI Agent operations. These solutions will enable desired economic outcomes and mitigate perceived risks. In short, by taking the full technical aspects of AI Agents seriously, one can see that although AI Agents are becoming more capable, existing technical and socio-legal governance, along with continual improvements in value-alignment, can allow AI Agents to meet the demands of law and society.

NOTE: An earlier working version of this paper is called Responsible AI Agents available at https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=5147666

detail.abstract: AI agents increasingly act with autonomy-selecting tools, invoking models, generating content, and executing multi-step workflows-yet no established legal or technical framework attributes their consequential actions to the humans and organizations that designed, deployed, and authorized them. This paper argues that agent autonomy cannot sever human and organizational accountability; it heightens the duty to make every consequential agent action attributable, scoped, reviewable, and remediable. The paper presents a transactional governance architecture, evaluated in an author-designed live test set on live infrastructure (DeBacco, 2026a-e), that produces a cryptographic receipt for every inference transaction-documenting the developer, deployer, authorizing principal, agent credential, intent classification, compliance outcome, and release or withhold decision. The receipt establishes an unbroken accountability chain from the human who authorized the agent to the specific inference that produced the output. Building on this architecture, the paper proposes a conditional safe-harbor framework: a developer or deployer may earn a rebuttable presumption of reasonable care only by proving that governance controls actually ran at the transaction boundary and that a verifiable record exists.¹ The conditions are demanding: non-bypassable controls, scoped authority, durable receipts, independent auditability, incident reporting, revocation, and remediation. A company that merely publishes a safety policy-or issues self-authenticated receipts-does not qualify. The paper synthesizes five prior publications establishing the engineering, theoretical, philosophical, legal, and empirical foundations of governed inference and demonstrates that the same accountability architecture extends to environmental governance: the organization that deploys an agent is accountable not only for what it does to people, but for the compute, energy, and carbon it authorizes the agent to consume. ¹ This paper proposes a conditional safe-harbor framework; it does not assert that a general statutory safe harbor for AI agents currently exists. Applicability is jurisdiction-specific and requires legal review.

detail.abstract: The changes to the metros are rapid and are driven by the need to deal with the ever growing demand from passengers, improve operational efficiency and ensure transportation security in increasingly complex urban environments. The reliability of services, protection of revenue and passVenger satisfaction remain compromised, however, due to recurring problems, such as fare evasion, passenger congestion, inadequate luggage management, accessibility issues for passengers with disabilities, and increasing cyber threats against electronic fare collection systems (Barabino et al., 2020; Cantillo et al., 2022). While many transit agencies have adopted one or more of these technologies-such as automated fare gates, contactless payment systems or surveillance systems-alone, the failure to adopt a coherent station architecture may prevent the system from being as effective and resilient as it could be (National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, 2022). In this research, the authors have tried to fill this gap by systematically synthesizing the latest literature and standards on contemporary international subway architecture, the latest cybersecurity standards, and the latest accessibility standards relating to subway architecture to create a comprehensive secure subway station architecture. The suggested framework includes one or more AI-driven fare verification systems, risk assessment-based passenger screening, contactless ticketing, secure digital payment systems, multi-layered cybersecurity protocols, privacy-focused data management, and universal accessibility standards to serve the smart transit goals of the 21st century (NIST, 2023; NIST, 2024). The results show the great benefit of having all of the four capabilities-physical security, intelligent automation, cybersecurity and inclusive infrastructure-integrated into a single architecture, which has a significant impact on revenue protection, passenger flow, threat detection, the reduction in operational inefficiencies, and equitable access for all passenger types. The potential design framework will give transit operators, transportation planners, infrastructure engineers and policy makers an easy-to-scale, standardsbased blueprint for creating secure, resilient and passenger friendly subway stations. The study also outlines future research opportunities that could leverage the use of digital twins, federated artificial intelligence, predictive crowd management, autonomous security monitoring and privacy enhancing technologies to further enhance the safety, sustainability and operational intelligence of future, next-generation, metropolitan rail networks (Barabino et al., 2020; NIST, 2024).

detail.abstract: Digital financial services, cloud banking, mobile payment systems, and real-time financial ecosystems have revolutionized the banking industry by making financial transactions quick and easy, and much more interconnected and accessible across the world (Chang et al., 2024; Zhu et al., 2024). This digital transformation has, at a time, also expanded the attack surface for cybercriminals, leading to more sophisticated financial fraud schemes like account takeover, synthetic identity fraud, payment fraud, insider threats and even AI-assisted attacks which are often hard to stop with traditional rule-based security systems (Nicholls et al., 2021; Dharmireddi et al., 2025). Current fraud detection methods often lack the ability to detect new attack patterns quickly and at the same time keep a low false-positive rate, are transparent in the model and are capable of a real-time decision making. It is proposed that a comprehensive hybrid Artificial Intelligence framework with the integration of every aforementioned AI methodology mentioned in this study can be used to boost financial fraud detection and response (Alarfaj & Shahzadi, 2025; Rahman, Nurujjaman, & Hossain, 2025; Waheed et al., 2026). This proposed framework integrates behavioral analytics, relational transaction modelling, ongoing policy optimization and interpretable AI methods to identify known and unknown fraudulent activities in financial environments comprised of distributed applications. The framework combines adaptive threat intelligence and reinforcement learning, enabling it to continuously adapt its detection methodologies in response to new attack behaviors and ensuring transparency for regulatory compliance and trust building among stakeholders. The anticipated results are that fraud detection will be more accurate, false positive rates will be minimized, models will be more explainable, models will be deployed across financial infrastructures in the cloud, and they will continuously learn to improve the overall organizational cyber resilience to enable secure digital financial operations in complex financial ecosystems (Rahmati, 2025; Kumar, 2025; Muthukumarasamy & Srinivasan, 2025).

title: Beyond AI Slop: Preparing Law Students for Responsible Practice in the AI Era
affiliations: University of Missouri School of Law

detail.title: Beyond AI Slop: Preparing Law Students for Responsible Practice in the AI Era

declarations.declarationOfInterest: I have no personal or financial relationship with anyone or organization that may have or could be perceived to influence this publication.
declarations.funderStatement: I have not received any funding to produce this publication.

detail.abstract:
People increasingly use artificial intelligence (AI) in legal matters.  Some AI-generated material is excellent.   But some is “AI slop”:  superficially impressive material that is inaccurate, misleading, or otherwise unreliable.  Slop can create problems not only for people who rely on it but also for lawyers, courts, mediators, and others who must determine what is reliable and what is not.  As AI use grows, these problems are likely to grow as well.

This article argues that law schools should prepare students for lawyers’ broad professional responsibilities in the AI era.  Future lawyers need to know how to use AI responsibly themselves, evaluate AI-generated material produced by others, and counsel clients about their own AI use.  These responsibilities require technological competence as well as independent professional judgment, risk-based verification, protection of confidential and sensitive information, and effective client counseling.

Law schools should develop coordinated, school-wide strategies to help students develop these competencies rather than relying primarily on isolated courses, individual faculty policies, or students learning about AI on their own.  Schools can use orientation programs, legal research and writing courses, clinics, simulations, specialized courses, workshops, library programs, and other activities.  Every law school should consider what graduates need to know and be able to do, where students will learn and practice those competencies, how their competence will be assessed, and how the program will evolve as AI and legal practice change.  Schools should adapt their strategies to their own circumstances.

title: Typed Decisions at the Edge: A Privacy-Preserving Hybrid Architecture for Everyday Decision Support, with an Early Product-Grounded Evaluation of System-One Decision Models

detail.title: Typed Decisions at the Edge: A Privacy-Preserving Hybrid Architecture for Everyday Decision Support, with an Early Product-Grounded Evaluation of System-One Decision Models

detail.abstract:
People make the same small decisions every day — what to eat, what to wear, what to train, what to study — and in low-connectivity settings any assistant for these decisions must work offline first. We describe Decide, a deployed feature of the open-source Khmer-language app iAny, built as a three-layer hybrid: a deterministic on-device scorer over a personal habit log; an optional remote "typed decision" model consulted only when the local scorer is unsure; and an acceptance gate that discards uninformative remote answers. The architecture rests on a wire format in which nothing user-authored crosses the network: candidates are described only by a closed tag vocabulary, situations only by bucketed enums, and identifiers are per-request ordinals. This single design choice yields three properties at once: a non-multilingual model can serve Khmer users, because language never crosses the wire; response caches are shareable across users, because identical situations produce identical keys; and the enumerable key space makes the cache exportable as an offline decision pack (within provider licensing). Decide ships in iAny today; it has not yet been the subject of any field study.

The week TypeSafe's Jev became publicly available (early access announced 15 September 2026; open access 21 September 2026) we ran an early product-grounded measurement of the category: twelve scenarios generated by the production code, sent unmodified to Jev and to the open-source Laya, judged by the same acceptance gate as production traffic. Jev answered 12/12, matched the deterministic scorer on 9/12, passed all four probes with predetermined correct answers (one, the honesty probe, sits exactly on the acceptance boundary and its verdict flips across repeated runs), and — most usefully — disagreed with the device on three judgment calls where, on our own inspection, the hand-tuned weights were wrong and the model was right; a comparison column for Laya is reported with its distribution-shift caveats. The pilot is small and author-scored. What it supports — rather than proves — is a practitioner's working conclusion: the deterministic layer is the most reliable component, the frontier model was the most reliable judge on this workload, and the gated hybrid inherits the strengths of both. The harness, payloads, and raw results are in the public repository.

detail.abstract:
Ask a training provider's booking system for "four places at the river campus in May" and something has to turn that sentence into a database query. Increasingly that something is a language model, called from code with nobody checking its work.

It fails in a way that is easy to miss. The model understands you perfectly and writes the river campus — but the catalogue lists that site as riverside. The meaning is right and the word is wrong, and because the query filters on exact values rather than approximate ones, and every stated constraint has to hold at once, one unmatched word returns nothing at all. You get an empty result rather than an error.

The usual advice is to make the model fill in a structured form instead of answering freely. That advice quietly contains two separate fixes: giving the model a form, and showing it the list of values the form will accept. We tested them separately, across 200 requests with three independent runs each.

Neither helps much on its own. Together they change the system's character. Asked questions it has everything it needs to answer, it replies "I need more information" 81% of the time with the form alone, and 4% with both — delivering a combined gain roughly three times what the two fixes predict on their own.

A control confirms the cause: when someone happens to phrase a request in the catalogue's own words, the advantage disappears entirely. This is not really about structure. It is about the distance between the words people use and the words a catalogue is indexed under.

One further result matters more than either: when the filtering is done by ordinary code rather than by the model, wrong results fall by 95% (from 2.07 to 0.11 per answered query) and answer quality doubles.

The catalogue and requests are synthetic and released with the study, so the correct answer to every request is computable rather than judged. No language model judges any result at any point. Generator, catalogue, harness and every raw result: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22907233

detail.abstract: Despite the central role of corporate tax departments in managing multinational enterprises' (MNEs) global tax positions, little is known about how their internal design shapes corporate tax behavior. Drawing on hand-collected data on more than 8,000 tax employees across 309 publicly listed European MNEs, we examine the association between tax department centralization and firm-level tax outcomes. We find no evidence for tax department centralization being associated with the overall level of tax planning. However, firms with more centralized tax departments engage in greater cross-border profit shifting, respond less to local tax incentives, and face higher tax risk. These findings suggest that tax department design shapes the means rather than the intensity of corporate tax planning. Our study extends the emerging literature on tax department design and provides insights for managers responsible for corporate tax strategies as well as for policymakers anticipating organizational responses to international tax reforms.

detail.title: Competition policy, industrial policy, and the allocative wedge: Rebuilding Hungary's competitiveness *

detail.abstract: Hungary's 2026 political transition presents an opportunity, and a challenge, to rebuild the institutional foundations of long-term competitiveness. This article examines the relationship between competition policy and industrial policy as two candidate policy instruments in the recovery process, through the lens of both contemporary economic research and Hungary's recent experience. Looking at data for Hungary and thirteen European comparator countries between 2005 and 2022, we provide evidence of the erosion of competitive market allocation, with weakening links between firm productivity and market shares, accompanied by increasingly concentrated markets and a rise in market power. Together, these findings are consistent with a weakening of allocative efficiency, through the weaker relationship between productivity, market share, and pricing power coinciding with the expansion of politically mediated allocation mechanisms documented over the same period. Given this institutional starting point, we argue that, for increased competitiveness, a balanced approach is needed for competition and industrial policies, to restore market competition and improve the efficiency of resource allocation on one side, and using modern, Draghi-style industrial policy aimed at supporting long-run productivity growth on the other.
